report:
### Conclusion
Yes, evidence indicates that olive leaf extract (OLE) can help lower high blood pressure, though findings across clinical trials vary.

### Summary of Evidence
* **Quantified BP Reductions:** Clinical evidence shows that taking 1000 mg/day of olive leaf extract may reduce systolic blood pressure by 11.45 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure by 4.65 mmHg (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ptr.8509).
* **Comparison to Medication:** In patients with stage-1 hypertension, OLE demonstrated blood pressure-lowering efficacy comparable to the prescription antihypertensive drug Captopril over eight weeks (https://naturalhealthresearch.org/olive-leaf-lowers-blood-pressure/).
* **Cardiovascular Health:** Extracts rich in olive phenolics, such as oleuropein, positively influence key cardiovascular risk factors by reducing high blood pressure and improving lipid profiles (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137474/).
* **Mixed Results:** Some clinical trials show less clear benefits. For instance, one double-blind study found OLE to be well-tolerated but observed no significant hypotensive benefit over placebo (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401757723_Evaluation_of_the_effect_of_olive_extracts_on_blood_pressure_and_cardiovascular_health_markers_in_adults_Findings_from_a_double-blind_placebo-controlled_randomised_trial).

Overall, while several studies support OLE's ability to reduce blood pressure, researchers note variable trial quality and emphasize the need for additional standardized clinical studies to confirm efficacy.
